actual_fields.evaluation_metrics: Q8 — EVALUATION METRICS, DATASET AND BASELINE  1. EVALUATION OBJECTIVE  The first release must establish a measurable and reproducible quality-evaluation framework for SupportIQ using synthetic/local-only evaluation data.  The evaluation must measure model quality, classification quality, citation reliability, structured-output validity, security enforcement, lifecycle enforcement, and response latency.  Model quality must be measured independently from human acceptance or override rates.  No metric may be declared passed without an explicitly defined scoring method, eligible denominator, evaluation dataset, and recorded evidence.  2. GROUNDED ANSWER QUALITY  Grounded-answer evaluation must measure whether generated answers are supported by eligible and authorized knowledge sources.  Each evaluated response must be assessed for:  - Factual support from retrieved sources. - Relevance to the user question. - Absence of unsupported factual claims. - Consistency with the available source material. - Compliance with applicable tenant and lifecycle restrictions.  The expected answer and supporting evidence must be defined in the evaluation dataset.  A response containing unsupported material claims must not be classified as fully grounded.  The exact scoring rubric and minimum acceptance threshold require explicit approval before the release gate can pass.  3. CITATION CORRECTNESS  Citation evaluation must establish whether each citation:  - References an existing source. - Identifies the correct document and relevant passage. - Supports the associated factual claim. - Belongs to the authorized tenant. - References knowledge eligible for AI retrieval at the evaluation anchor. - Does not reference expired, rejected, superseded, overdue, or deletion-approved content.  Citation correctness must be evaluated independently from answer relevance.  Invalid, unsupported, inaccessible, or incorrectly attributed citations must be counted as failures.  Citation scoring must use an explicitly defined eligible citation population.  4. ABSTENTION AND CONFLICT HANDLING  The evaluation dataset must include:  - Questions with insufficient supporting knowledge. - Questions with conflicting authoritative sources. - Questions outside the available knowledge scope. - Questions involving unauthorized tenant content. - Questions involving expired, overdue, or otherwise ineligible knowledge.  The evaluation must measure whether the assistant correctly abstains, explains insufficient evidence, or requests human review where required.  A confident but unsupported answer must count as an evaluation failure.  The system must not resolve restricted knowledge conflicts merely by generating an answer.  Human-review and lifecycle restrictions remain mandatory.  5. CLASSIFICATION QUALITY  Category, Priority, and Queue suggestion quality must be evaluated independently.  Each field must have an explicitly labelled expected synthetic reference value.  Measure:  - Category suggestion accuracy. - Priority suggestion accuracy. - Queue suggestion accuracy. - Missing or unassessed suggestion rates. - Invalid or unsupported suggestion rates.  Only eligible records with a valid reference label may enter the applicable accuracy denominator.  Unassessed and ineligible records must be reported separately.  Model prediction accuracy must not be confused with human acceptance, rejection, or override rates defined in Q7.  6. STRUCTURED-OUTPUT VALIDITY  All required structured outputs must be evaluated against their approved schemas.  Evaluation must include:  - Valid JSON or required output format. - Required field presence. - Correct field types. - Allowed enumeration values. - Required-field validation. - Null and missing-value handling. - Rejection of malformed or unsupported values.  Schema-valid output and semantically correct output must be reported as separate quality dimensions.  The evaluation schema must be version-controlled.  Undefined schema fields and validation requirements remain gated until explicitly approved.  7. TENANT ISOLATION AND LIFECYCLE ENFORCEMENT  Tenant isolation must be evaluated through positive and negative authorization tests.  The evaluation must verify that:  - Authorized tenant users can access only permitted tenant resources. - Cross-tenant document and knowledge retrieval is denied. - Unauthorized citations cannot expose another tenant's information. - Platform Admin permissions do not grant tenant-content access. - Restricted lifecycle states are excluded from AI retrieval and citation. - Overdue, rejected, expired, superseded, and deletion-approved knowledge cannot become eligible through an unrelated operation.  These are mandatory security and lifecycle evaluation dimensions.  Any confirmed unauthorized cross-tenant access or prohibited lifecycle retrieval must be treated as a release-blocking failure.  Passing average model-quality metrics must never compensate for security or lifecycle failures.  8. RESPONSE LATENCY EVALUATION  The first release may measure descriptive response latency using synthetic evaluation scenarios.  Report: - Median response latency (P50). - 95th percentile response latency (P95). - Evaluation sample count. - Evaluation environment. - Model and configuration version. - Relevant test conditions.  Latency must be measured using explicitly recorded timestamps and a consistent measurement boundary.  These are descriptive measurements, not production performance guarantees or contractual SLAs.  Minimum latency targets and production performance commitments remain deferred.  9. SYNTHETIC EVALUATION DATASET  Create a version-controlled synthetic evaluation dataset.  The dataset must contain:  - Evaluation case identifier. - Synthetic tenant identifier. - Input question or classification scenario. - Expected answer or reference classification. - Expected supporting source references. - Expected abstention or human-review behaviour, where applicable. - Expected structured-output schema. - Applicable lifecycle and authorization conditions. - Evaluation category and difficulty. - Expected outcome and scoring rubric.  Include normal, edge, negative, insufficient-evidence, conflicting-source, and unauthorized-access scenarios.  Every expected reference label must have identifiable provenance and review status.  The dataset must not contain real customer information or production tenant content.  Use an explicit dataset version, such as SupportIQ-Eval-v1.0.  Evaluation dataset changes must be version-controlled so that results from different versions are not silently compared as equivalent.  10. BASELINE AND SCORING GOVERNANCE  The initial evaluation baseline must be established through actual execution against an approved, versioned synthetic evaluation dataset.  Record:  - Dataset version. - Model and model configuration version. - Application build version. - Evaluation date and environment. - Metric definitions and scoring rubric versions. - Eligible population and denominators. - Raw evaluation results. - Excluded and invalid cases. - Failure classifications. - Evaluation evidence.  Aggregate scores must not hide field-level, tenant-isolation, citation, or lifecycle failures.  A baseline must not be invented or declared passed before the evaluation has actually been executed and independently reviewed.  11. HUMAN ACCEPTANCE VERSUS MODEL QUALITY  Model quality metrics and human decision metrics must remain separate.  Model quality measures the correctness of AI-generated answers and suggestions against independently prepared synthetic reference labels.  Human acceptance, rejection, and override rates measure completed human review decisions as defined in Q7-C02.  High human acceptance must not automatically establish model correctness.  Similarly, a model evaluation score must not replace independent human approval requirements.  12. QUALITY THRESHOLDS AND RELEASE GATES  Metric definitions and evaluation methodology are established first.  Numeric quality thresholds, minimum sample sizes, confidence requirements, and final release acceptance criteria must not be invented or assumed.  These values require explicit approval based on evaluation evidence and the intended release risk.  Until approved thresholds and corresponding evidence exist, the applicable quality gate must remain NOT EVALUATED or NOT APPROVED.  Security, tenant-isolation, authorization, and lifecycle enforcement failures are release-blocking regardless of aggregate model-quality scores.  13. EXPLICITLY DEFERRED ITEMS  The following remain deferred until separately defined and approved:  - Numeric model-quality acceptance thresholds. - Minimum evaluation sample sizes. - Statistical confidence requirements. - Production performance targets. - Production SLA commitments. - Actual customer-data evaluation. - Advanced model benchmarking. - Continuous production monitoring and drift thresholds. - Automated quality-based model promotion. - Production rollout and release authorization.  14. FINAL DECISION  The first release will establish a measurable evaluation framework using version-controlled synthetic/local-only data.  Grounded answers, citation correctness, abstention, classification quality, structured-output validity, tenant isolation, lifecycle enforcement, and response latency will be evaluated independently.  The initial baseline must come from actual recorded evaluation results, not assumed values.  Numeric acceptance thresholds and final release criteria remain explicit approval gates until supported by evidence and approved.  No quality gate may be marked passed merely because its metric, dataset, or test plan has been defined.  All Q1-Q7 security, authorization, tenant-isolation, lifecycle, retention, analytics, and no-external-action restrictions remain unchanged.  These decisions clarify evaluation requirements only. They do not authorize tests, implementation, PRD approval, or product release.
actual_fields.numeric_thresholds: Q8-C02 — NUMERIC ACCEPTANCE THRESHOLDS AND APPROVAL AUTHORITY  1. NUMERIC QUALITY THRESHOLDS  Do not invent or assume numeric acceptance thresholds for the first release.  The following metrics require explicitly approved numeric pass/fail criteria:  - Grounded answer accuracy. - Citation correctness. - Correct abstention and conflict handling. - Category suggestion accuracy. - Priority suggestion accuracy. - Queue suggestion accuracy. - Structured-output validity. - Response latency, including P50 and P95.  These thresholds must be proposed using actual evaluation evidence, dataset characteristics, business risk and the approved scoring methodology.  Until independently approved, these values remain PENDING and the corresponding quality release gates must remain NOT EVALUATED / NOT APPROVED.  2. CRITICAL SECURITY AND SAFETY THRESHOLDS  The following are mandatory zero-tolerance release conditions:  - Confirmed cross-tenant data leakage. - Unauthorized tenant-content access. - Unauthorized knowledge retrieval or citation. - Retrieval of deletion-approved or otherwise prohibited knowledge. - Bypass of tenant authorization or lifecycle restrictions. - Platform Admin access to tenant content. - Unauthorized approval, reinstatement or privilege escalation.  Any confirmed critical violation is a release-blocking failure, regardless of aggregate quality scores or other passing metrics.  A zero-tolerance policy means zero confirmed violations in the applicable evaluation. It does not imply that finite testing mathematically proves the absence of every possible vulnerability.  3. SAMPLE SIZE AND TEST COVERAGE  Minimum evaluation sample sizes, category-wise coverage, negative-test coverage, statistical confidence requirements and test repetition criteria remain PENDING.  These must be proposed based on:  - Evaluation dataset size and representativeness. - Metric-specific eligible populations. - Risk and severity of failure. - Coverage of normal, boundary and negative scenarios. - Tenant-isolation and lifecycle test coverage. - Reproducibility of evaluation results.  A release must not be considered passed merely because a small or incomplete sample produces favourable results.  4. LATENCY ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA  P50 and P95 latency must be measured and recorded using a consistent measurement boundary.  Numeric latency targets, concurrency assumptions, load profiles, hardware/runtime environment and performance acceptance criteria remain PENDING.  Descriptive latency measurements must not be represented as production SLA commitments.  5. PROPOSAL AND INDEPENDENT APPROVAL AUTHORITY  The proposed governance arrangement is:  - Product Owner / Quality Owner: Proposes metric definitions, numeric acceptance thresholds, dataset coverage and evaluation methodology. - Independent Release Approver: Reviews the supporting evidence and independently approves or rejects the proposed quality acceptance criteria. - Security Owner: Independently reviews and approves security-critical acceptance criteria, including tenant isolation, authorization and lifecycle enforcement. - Engineering Team: Provides implementation evidence, test results and technical recommendations but cannot independently approve its own release acceptance results.  The person proposing a threshold must not be its sole final approver.  The exact accountable individuals and formal role assignments must be recorded before the relevant approval gate is activated.  Administrative privileges alone must not confer Knowledge Reviewer authority or tenant-content access.  6. RELEASE BLOCKING BOUNDARY  Until numeric quality thresholds, minimum sample sizes, evaluation coverage and independent approval authority are explicitly documented and approved:  - The relevant quality acceptance gate remains PENDING. - No missing threshold may be treated as an implicit pass. - No aggregate score may override a critical security failure. - No quality result may be represented as independently approved without recorded approval evidence. - Production release authorization remains separate from metric definition and evaluation planning.  7. EXPLICITLY DEFERRED DECISIONS  The following remain unresolved and require separate approval:  - Exact numeric thresholds for each quality metric. - Minimum evaluation sample sizes. - Statistical confidence and coverage requirements. - P50/P95 latency targets and load conditions. - Named individuals assigned to approval roles. - Final release acceptance criteria.  RATIONALE:  The first release should establish evidence-based quality governance rather than arbitrary numerical targets.  Security and authorization violations require zero-tolerance treatment, while model-quality thresholds should be based on reproducible evaluation results and independently approved acceptance criteria.  This decision records the intended governance boundary only. It does not approve the PRD, authorize implementation, approve testing execution or authorize product release.  All previously established Q1-Q7 restrictions remain unchanged.
actual_fields.evidence_ownership: Q8-C03 — EVALUATION EVIDENCE OWNER AND CONFIGURATION BINDING  1. EVIDENCE PREPARATION  The Engineering and QA teams are responsible for preparing evaluation evidence.  They must execute the approved evaluation suite against the explicitly identified application build, model configuration, synthetic dataset and policy versions.  Evidence must include:  - Test execution records. - Evaluation dataset and version. - Metric definitions and scoring methodology. - Expected and actual results. - Pass/fail outcomes. - Failed and excluded test cases with reasons. - Security and lifecycle test results. - Relevant logs and reproducible execution references.  The team preparing evidence must not independently approve its own release evidence.  2. INDEPENDENT VERIFICATION AND REVIEW  An independent QA / Quality Reviewer must verify:  - Correctness and completeness of the evaluation execution. - Dataset and expected-reference integrity. - Scoring methodology and denominator calculations. - Reproducibility of reported results. - Correct application and configuration versions. - Completeness of failed, excluded and unresolved test cases. - Security and lifecycle evaluation evidence.  The reviewer must be independent of the evidence preparation and must not approve their own work.  3. EVIDENCE ACCEPTANCE AND RELEASE AUTHORITY  An authorized Independent Release Approver is responsible for accepting or rejecting the final evaluation evidence.  The Security Owner must independently review security-critical evidence, including tenant isolation, authorization and lifecycle enforcement.  The final human release decision must consider:  - Approved acceptance thresholds. - Verified evaluation evidence. - Critical security and lifecycle results. - Open defects and unresolved exceptions. - Applicable approval and SDLC gates.  Evidence acceptance does not itself authorize production deployment or implementation.  The exact named individuals and formal role assignments must be established through the applicable governance approval process.  4. CONFIGURATION BINDING  Every evaluation execution must be bound to an immutable configuration manifest containing, where applicable:  APPLICATION: - Application version and build identifier. - Git commit ID and relevant release candidate. - Relevant dependency and configuration versions.  AI MODEL: - AI provider. - Model name and exact model version. - Model parameters and relevant inference configuration.  PROMPT: - System prompt version. - Prompt template and configuration version. - Relevant generation settings.  RETRIEVAL AND KNOWLEDGE: - Retrieval configuration and parameters. - Embedding model and version. - Vector index version. - Chunking and indexing configuration. - Synthetic knowledge dataset version and snapshot identifier.  BUSINESS AND SECURITY POLICIES: - Taxonomy and category mapping version. - Priority and routing rule versions. - Tenant authorization policy version. - Knowledge lifecycle policy version.  EVALUATION: - Evaluation dataset version. - Test suite version. - Metric definition and scoring rubric versions. - Execution timestamp and environment. - Raw results and final evaluation report.  Sensitive credentials, secrets and actual customer content must never be included in evaluation evidence.  5. CONFIGURATION CHANGE AND RE-EVALUATION RULES  A new evaluation is required whenever a change materially affects the validity of previous evidence.  Examples include:  - AI provider, model or model-version changes. - System prompt or generation configuration changes. - Embedding, retrieval, indexing or chunking changes. - Knowledge source or evaluation dataset changes. - Taxonomy, priority or routing rule changes. - Tenant authorization or lifecycle policy changes. - Application changes affecting retrieval, answer generation, classification, security or evaluation behaviour.  The required re-evaluation scope must be determined through documented impact analysis.  Security, authorization and lifecycle changes must trigger the applicable security and lifecycle regression tests.  A change that invalidates previous evidence must not inherit an earlier passing result without fresh verification.  Evidence remains traceable to its original configuration even after newer versions are introduced.  6. FAILURE AND EXCEPTION HANDLING  Failed evaluations must remain recorded and must not be silently removed, overwritten or reported as passing.  Every failure must include:  - Test case identifier. - Affected metric or control. - Expected result. - Actual result. - Failure severity. - Relevant configuration. - Investigation status. - Corrective action and verification evidence.  Any exception requires documented justification, explicit scope and approval by the authorized human authority.  Critical security, tenant-isolation, authorization and prohibited-lifecycle failures cannot be waived through aggregate quality scores or informal exceptions.  Unresolved critical failures must block the applicable release gate.  7. EVIDENCE RETENTION AND TRACEABILITY  Evaluation evidence must be version-controlled and traceable to the exact configuration that produced it.  Evidence records must preserve their original execution context and approval history.  Evidence retention duration and detailed archival or purge implementation remain subject to the applicable retention policy and approval requirements.  No evidence may be modified retrospectively to conceal a failure or change an earlier approval decision.  8. SEPARATION OF SDLC GATES  The following activities remain separate:  - Evaluation planning. - Evaluation execution. - Independent evidence verification. - Acceptance of evaluation evidence. - Requirement approval. - Implementation authorization. - Production release authorization.  Completing one stage does not automatically approve or authorize the next stage.  No clarification or evidence acceptance in this question grants permission to begin implementation, modify the PRD, deploy software or initiate another SDLC process.  9. EXPLICITLY DEFERRED ITEMS  The following remain pending:  - Named individuals assigned to each governance role. - Final approval delegation and escalation arrangements. - Exact evidence retention duration. - Detailed configuration manifest schema. - Automated configuration-drift detection. - Automated re-evaluation and evidence invalidation workflows. - Formal release approval workflow and tooling.  RATIONALE:  The first release must provide reproducible, independently verifiable evaluation evidence.  Binding every result to its exact software, AI, prompt, retrieval, dataset and policy configuration prevents outdated test results from being incorrectly reused after material changes.  Independent verification and human release authority preserve separation of duties and SDLC governance.  All previously established Q1-Q7 restrictions and Q8 acceptance-threshold requirements remain unchanged.  These decisions clarify governance and evidence requirements only. They do not approve the PRD, authorize implementation, authorize test execution or approve production release.
actual_fields.citations: Q8-C04 — CITATION IDENTITY, DISPLAY AND SAFE FALLBACK  1. STABLE CITATION IDENTITY  Every citation must reference a stable, tenant-scoped source identity.  The minimum identity must include:  - Tenant identifier. - Document identifier. - Exact document version identifier. - Source location identifier, where available. - Relevant page, section or chunk reference, where available.  A citation must resolve to the exact source version used during answer generation.  A document identifier alone is not sufficient to establish that the cited content supports an answer.  A citation must remain distinguishable from references to other versions of the same logical document.  2. HUMAN-READABLE CITATION DISPLAY  Where available and authorized, the user-facing citation should display:  - Document title. - Document version. - Relevant page number. - Section name. - Relevant source excerpt or supporting passage. - Accessible source reference.  Display metadata must be derived from the actual indexed document and its recorded metadata.  The system must never invent document titles, version numbers, page numbers, section names or source references.  3. MISSING OR INCOMPLETE METADATA  If a document title is unavailable, use a safe document reference only if that reference is authorized for display.  If a page number, section name or other location metadata is unavailable, explicitly indicate that the information is unavailable.  Do not substitute guessed page numbers, inferred section names or fabricated metadata.  If the source cannot be identified reliably, do not present the citation as verified.  4. SOURCE ACCESSIBILITY AND SAFE FALLBACK  Before displaying a citation or providing an accessible source link, verify that:  - The source belongs to the requesting tenant. - The requesting user is authorized to access it. - The exact cited version remains eligible for AI retrieval and citation. - The cited source location is valid. - The supporting evidence is available and actually supports the associated claim.  If the original source is unavailable, inaccessible, or cannot be verified, the assistant must not manufacture a replacement reference.  Where citation evidence is insufficient, the assistant must qualify the answer, abstain from unsupported claims or request human review as appropriate.  Human authorization to inspect a document is separate from AI retrieval and citation eligibility.  5. CITATION AND SOURCE-VERSION RESTRICTIONS  The assistant must never cite:  - Expired documents. - Rejected documents. - Superseded versions. - Overdue knowledge pending re-review. - Deletion-approved content. - Unauthorized tenant content. - Sources that fail applicable lifecycle or authorization checks.  A valid-looking document reference does not prove that its contents support the generated answer.  An older version must not be cited merely because it remains stored.  Existing Q1-Q5 lifecycle, approval, retention and deletion restrictions remain mandatory.  6. CITATION VALIDATION  Citation evaluation must independently verify:  - Correct tenant identity. - Correct document identity. - Correct document version. - Correct source location. - Actual support for the associated factual claim. - Current retrieval eligibility. - User authorization. - Source accessibility.  A citation that points to the correct document but an irrelevant or unsupported passage must be treated as incorrect.  Citation identity validity and citation evidence correctness must remain separate evaluation dimensions.  7. AUDITABILITY AND TRACEABILITY  Each generated citation must be traceable to its original retrieval context and exact document version.  Where applicable, retain:  - Citation identifier. - Tenant and document identifiers. - Document version. - Source location and chunk identifier. - Retrieval execution reference. - Citation validation outcome. - Applicable policy version.  Audit records must not expose confidential source content or unauthorized tenant metadata.  8. EXPLICITLY DEFERRED ITEMS  The following implementation details remain subject to further design and approval:  - Final citation display format. - Exact metadata schema. - Citation-link expiration and access-refresh behaviour. - Source excerpt display limits. - Behaviour when the original document is archived or physically unavailable. - Detailed citation audit retention implementation. - User-interface treatment of unavailable citations.  These details must not be filled with assumed defaults.  RATIONALE:  The first release must provide trustworthy, traceable and tenant-safe citations.  The system must prioritize source accuracy and authorization over displaying a citation for every generated answer.  A missing citation must never be replaced by fabricated metadata or an unauthorized alternative source.  All previously established Q1-Q7 restrictions and Q8 evaluation governance requirements remain unchanged.  This clarification does not approve the PRD, authorize implementation, testing execution or production release.
actual_fields.structured_outputs: Q8-C05 — REQUIRED STRUCTURED RESPONSE CONTRACTS  1. FIRST-RELEASE RESPONSE TYPES  The first release must define versioned structured response contracts for the following response types:  A. ANSWER / ABSTENTION - Generated answer. - Supporting evidence references. - Citation references. - Evidence sufficiency status. - Uncertainty indicators. - Abstention reason, where applicable. - Human-review requirement.  B. SUMMARY - Summary text. - Source document and version references. - Supporting evidence references. - Missing or unavailable information indicators. - Uncertainty or qualification markers.  C. CATEGORY SUGGESTION - Suggested category identifier and value. - Explanation. - Supporting evidence. - Confidence or uncertainty indicator. - Human-review status.  D. PRIORITY SUGGESTION - Suggested priority value. - Explanation and supporting evidence. - Confidence or uncertainty indicator. - Human-review status.  E. QUEUE SUGGESTION - Suggested synthetic/local queue identifier. - Explanation and supporting evidence. - Uncertainty indicator. - Human-review status.  F. ESCALATION RECOMMENDATION - Whether human escalation is recommended. - Reason and supporting evidence. - Suggested escalation category, where defined. - Uncertainty and review requirements.  Escalation recommendations must never automatically modify tickets, queues, assignments or external systems.  2. COMMON REQUIRED RESPONSE FIELDS  Where applicable, every structured response must include:  - ResponseId. - ResponseType. - SchemaVersion. - ResponseStatus. - SuggestedValue. - Explanation. - EvidenceReferences. - CitationReferences. - ConfidenceIndicator, where supported. - UncertaintyMarkers. - HumanReviewRequired. - GeneratedTimestamp. - Applicable tenant and authorization context.  Fields must be appropriate to the response type.  Unavailable values must be represented explicitly according to the approved schema rather than fabricated or silently substituted.  3. STATUS VALUES AND SEMANTICS  The following status values are proposed:  - SUGGESTED: AI-generated recommendation. - NEEDS_REVIEW: Human review is required. - ACCEPTED: Explicitly accepted by an authorized human reviewer. - REJECTED: Explicitly rejected by an authorized human reviewer. - OVERRIDDEN: An authorized human has replaced the suggested value. - UNASSESSED: Insufficient information to make an assessment. - ABSTAINED: The assistant deliberately abstained from providing an unsupported answer.  AI-generated responses may create SUGGESTED, NEEDS_REVIEW, UNASSESSED or ABSTAINED outcomes as applicable.  ACCEPTED, REJECTED and OVERRIDDEN must originate only from authorized human decisions.  An AI suggestion must never be represented as an authoritative human decision.  4. EVIDENCE, UNCERTAINTY AND REVIEW MARKERS  Every response must distinguish:  - Supported claims. - Unsupported or insufficiently supported claims. - Missing source information. - Conflicting evidence. - Unavailable citations. - Restricted or ineligible knowledge. - Human-review requirements.  Confidence indicators must not be interpreted as proof of factual correctness.  Where evidence is insufficient or conflicting, the assistant must qualify its response, abstain or request human review as appropriate.  Restricted tenant content and lifecycle-ineligible knowledge must never be used to populate response evidence.  5. STRICT SCHEMA VALIDATION  All structured responses must be validated against their exact approved, versioned schemas.  Validation must cover:  - Required fields. - Field data types. - Allowed enumerations. - Null and missing-value behaviour. - Response-type-specific requirements. - Evidence and citation references. - Status transition restrictions. - Tenant and authorization context. - Schema version compatibility.  Malformed, incomplete or unsupported outputs must not be silently accepted.  A schema-valid response must not automatically be considered factually correct.  Schema validation and semantic evaluation must remain separate quality dimensions.  6. SCHEMA VERSIONING AND APPROVAL  Each response contract must have an explicit version identifier.  Schema definitions, allowed enums, required fields and validation rules must be version-controlled.  The exact response schemas and their approval status must be established before affected implementation and formal evaluation proceed.  Changes to an approved schema must be versioned and assessed for backward compatibility.  A material schema change must trigger the applicable regression and evaluation activities.  No implementation or evaluation gate may assume an unapproved schema.  7. HUMAN DECISION AND AUTOMATION BOUNDARIES  AI-generated structured responses are recommendations only.  The assistant must not automatically:  - Accept or reject knowledge. - Approve document versions. - Change authoritative classifications. - Update ticket fields. - Change ticket ownership or assignments. - Modify external queues. - Trigger escalation workflows. - Send outgoing messages. - Perform external write operations.  All authoritative decisions must remain with the appropriately authorized human roles established in Q2, Q3, Q4 and Q6.  Human decisions must be independently auditable and distinguishable from original AI suggestions.  8. FIRST-RELEASE TAXONOMY AND ENUM DEPENDENCIES  Category, Priority and Queue enumerations must reference the approved Q6 taxonomy and mapping definitions.  Do not invent or hardcode unapproved category, priority or queue values.  Unsupported, ambiguous or unavailable values must be represented through explicitly approved fallback or UNASSESSED behaviour.  The response schema must not independently create new business categories or bypass Q6 approval requirements.  9. EXPLICITLY DEFERRED ITEMS  The following require separate design and approval:  - Exact JSON Schema definitions. - Final schema versions. - Complete response-type-specific field definitions. - Final enum values and fallback mappings. - Confidence-score representation and calibration. - Detailed error-response contracts. - Backward-compatibility and migration rules. - Exact schema approval roles. - Automated schema compatibility testing.  Until approved, affected implementation and evaluation must remain gated.  RATIONALE:  Structured response contracts provide predictable, machine-validatable AI outputs while preserving the distinction between AI recommendations and authoritative human decisions.  Strict schema validation improves integration reliability, auditability and future extensibility.  Separating output structure from decision authority prevents AI-generated suggestions from silently becoming operational actions.  All Q1-Q7 restrictions and Q8 evaluation governance requirements remain unchanged.  These decisions clarify requirements only. They do not approve the PRD, authorize implementation, testing execution or production release.
actual_fields.retry_rejection: Q8-C06 — SAFE RETRY, REJECTION AND FAILURE VISIBILITY  1. GENERAL FAILURE-HANDLING PRINCIPLE  The first release must follow a fail-safe approach.  When an operation cannot be completed reliably, the system must explicitly report failure, abstain or request human review rather than fabricate success or return unsupported results.  Retry must be bounded and permitted only for explicitly classified transient failures.  Security, authorization, tenant-isolation and lifecycle restrictions must never be bypassed during retry or recovery.  2. FAILURES PERMITTING BOUNDED RETRY  The following transient failures may permit a bounded retry:  - Temporary network interruptions. - AI provider transient service errors. - Temporary provider rate limiting. - Transient dependency unavailability. - Recoverable infrastructure timeouts.  Retries must use an explicitly approved retry policy with configurable limits, appropriate backoff and timeout handling.  Idempotency and duplicate-request protection must be maintained wherever applicable.  Exact retry counts, backoff intervals, timeout values and circuit-breaker thresholds remain pending technical design and approval.  3. INVALID SCHEMA AND MALFORMED OUTPUT  If an AI response fails structured schema validation:  - Reject the invalid output. - A bounded corrective retry may be considered where safe and supported. - Revalidate the complete response against the exact approved schema. - Do not expose malformed output as a successful response. - Do not silently discard missing required fields or invent replacement values.  If validation continues to fail, mark the operation as FAILED and expose an appropriate error or human-review requirement.  Schema-valid output must still undergo applicable semantic and evidence validation.  4. MISSING CITATIONS AND INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE  Missing, invalid or unsupported citations must not be treated as successful grounded answers.  If citation evidence is unavailable:  - Abstain from unsupported factual claims. - Return an appropriately qualified response where partial support exists. - Identify missing evidence where possible. - Request human review when required.  Insufficient or conflicting evidence must not trigger unlimited retries or automatic selection of an unsupported source.  5. SECURITY, AUTHORIZATION AND LIFECYCLE FAILURES  The following conditions require immediate rejection or blocking without retry:  - Unauthorized access. - Cross-tenant access attempts. - Tenant authorization failures. - Prohibited lifecycle-state retrieval. - Expired, rejected or superseded knowledge. - Overdue knowledge excluded from AI retrieval. - Deletion-approved content. - Unauthorized approval or reinstatement attempts.  These conditions must not be converted into transient errors.  No retry, fallback, alternate provider or reprocessing mechanism may bypass authorization, tenant isolation, deletion or lifecycle controls.  Confirmed security violations must be recorded for appropriate security investigation and escalation.  6. UNAVAILABLE DEPENDENCIES  If the AI provider, retrieval service, vector index, database or another required dependency becomes unavailable:  - Do not report successful processing without verified completion. - Permit bounded retries only for classified transient failures. - Return a clear service-unavailable or processing-failed outcome. - Preserve the request correlation identifier. - Avoid duplicate processing or inconsistent partial results. - Expose the failure to authorized operational personnel.  If a required dependency remains unavailable, the affected operation must remain FAILED or otherwise explicitly unresolved.  7. DELETION AND PURGE SAFEGUARDS  Deletion-approved content must never be reprocessed or restored through retry, recovery, indexing or alternate processing paths.  A failed purge must remain visibly incomplete.  Retry ownership, escalation and deletion verification must follow the approved Q5 deletion and retention requirements.  The system must never report successful deletion before the applicable deletion operation has been verified.  8. FAILURE STATUS AND VISIBILITY  The system must distinguish at least the following operational outcomes:  - SUCCESS: Operation completed and validated. - RETRYING: A permitted transient retry is in progress. - FAILED: Operation could not be completed. - REJECTED: Input or operation was rejected by validation or policy. - ABSTAINED: Assistant deliberately declined to provide an unsupported answer. - NEEDS_REVIEW: Human intervention is required. - BLOCKED: Operation was prevented by authorization, security or lifecycle restrictions.  These operational statuses must remain separate from authoritative knowledge lifecycle and human approval statuses.  A technical retry must not automatically change an approval or lifecycle decision.  9. FAILURE VISIBILITY AND AUDITABILITY  For end users, provide a clear and safe explanation of the failure, including whether retry or human review is appropriate.  For authorized administrators and support personnel, record:  - Correlation ID and request identifier. - Failure category and error code. - Relevant operation and dependency. - Timestamp. - Retry attempt information. - Final processing status. - Applicable configuration version. - Resolution or escalation status.  Do not expose credentials, API keys, confidential source content, internal secrets or unauthorized tenant information in error messages or logs.  Failure logs must be tenant-safe and accessible only to appropriately authorized roles.  10. EXPLICITLY DEFERRED ITEMS  The following require separate technical definition and approval:  - Exact retry counts. - Backoff intervals. - Provider-specific timeout values. - Circuit-breaker configuration. - Retry ownership and operational escalation. - Dead-letter and failed-request handling. - Detailed error-code catalogue. - Automated recovery workflows. - Failure-log retention and monitoring thresholds.  Until approved, these values must not be silently assumed or treated as implemented guarantees.  RATIONALE:  The first release must prioritize correctness, security and transparent failure handling over uninterrupted processing.  Transient technical failures may receive bounded retries, while authorization, tenant-isolation, lifecycle and deletion violations require immediate blocking.  An explicit failure or abstention is preferable to an apparently successful but unsupported answer.  All previously established Q1-Q7 restrictions and Q8 evaluation requirements remain unchanged.  These decisions clarify requirements only. They do not approve the PRD, authorize implementation, testing execution or production release.
actual_fields.rationale_deferrals: Q8-C07 — RATIONALE AND EXPLICIT UNRESOLVED RELEASE GATES  1. FIRST-RELEASE POLICY AND RATIONALE  The first demonstrable release of SupportIQ must remain within the previously established synthetic/local-only, read-only and restricted integration boundary.  The purpose of this release is to demonstrate the core product capabilities while establishing measurable quality, security, governance and operational evidence.  The first release may demonstrate:  - AI-generated answers and summaries using eligible synthetic knowledge. - Tenant-scoped knowledge retrieval and citation. - Category, Priority and Queue suggestions. - Human-review and approval workflows. - Structured response validation. - Synthetic analytics and evaluation reporting. - Safe failure, abstention and bounded retry behaviour.  The system must not introduce real customer data, unrestricted production integrations, automatic ticket changes, outgoing messages or unauthorized external actions.  These restrictions provide a controlled environment in which the product can be evaluated without assuming that synthetic demonstrations prove production readiness.  2. QUALITY AND EVALUATION POLICY  Evaluation must be based on version-controlled synthetic datasets and explicitly defined scoring methodology.  Actual evaluation results must be recorded and independently reviewed.  No numeric quality threshold, performance target, statistical confidence level or minimum sample size may be invented or assumed.  Security, tenant isolation, authorization and lifecycle violations remain mandatory release-blocking conditions.  A favourable aggregate model-quality score cannot compensate for a critical security or authorization failure.  3. EVIDENCE AND CONFIGURATION GOVERNANCE  Evaluation evidence must be bound to the exact application build, Git commit, AI provider/model version, prompt configuration, retrieval settings, dataset version, taxonomy and applicable policy versions.  Evidence must be independently verified and accepted by authorized human roles.  Material configuration changes must trigger impact assessment and the applicable re-evaluation.  Acceptance of evaluation evidence remains separate from Requirement approval, implementation authorization and production release approval.  4. EXPLICITLY UNRESOLVED DECISIONS  The following decisions remain pending and must not be silently assumed:  A. QUALITY AND EVALUATION - Numeric pass/fail thresholds for each applicable quality metric. - Minimum evaluation sample sizes and coverage. - Statistical confidence and acceptance requirements. - P50/P95 latency targets and load conditions. - Final quality acceptance criteria.  B. RESPONSE CONTRACTS AND DATASETS - Exact approved structured-response schemas and versions. - Final taxonomy and enum definitions where not already approved. - Complete synthetic evaluation dataset and reference-label approval. - Final citation metadata and display contracts. - Detailed error and failure-response contracts.  C. GOVERNANCE AND PERMISSIONS - Named individuals assigned to evidence preparation, independent verification, security review and release approval. - Final approval delegation and escalation arrangements. - Exact permissions for any future runtime or live integration. - Formal evidence acceptance and release authorization records.  D. TECHNICAL AND OPERATIONAL POLICY - Retry counts, backoff and timeout settings. - Final latency and performance acceptance conditions. - Detailed monitoring and recovery arrangements. - Evidence retention and archival implementation. - Automated configuration-drift and re-evaluation mechanisms.  E. RETENTION AND LIFECYCLE - Previously deferred Q5 retention schedules and affected capability approval gates remain unresolved. - No retention deferral implies permission to retain, retrieve or reprocess prohibited content.  5. PB-02 PORTABILITY CONDITION  PB-02 remains an explicit unresolved approval gate.  The synthetic/local-only boundary does not automatically establish that the system is safe or authorized for runtime, production, external-provider or live-integration operation.  Before any affected runtime, live integration or release boundary proceeds, the following must be explicitly defined and approved:  - Exact connector/provider permissions. - Exact permitted data reads and operations. - Tenant and user authorization boundaries. - Applicable approved quality thresholds. - Required security and evaluation evidence. - Independent verification and approval records. - Applicable failure, retry and lifecycle safeguards.  No write, message-sending or external-action permission may be inferred from a read-only or synthetic demonstration.  If these conditions are not satisfied, the affected capability must remain blocked or deferred.  6. RELEASE GATE ENFORCEMENT  The following boundaries must remain separate:  - Requirement clarification. - Requirement approval. - Technical design approval. - Implementation authorization. - Test execution authorization. - Evaluation evidence acceptance. - Runtime and live-integration authorization. - Production deployment and release approval.  Completion of Q8 does not automatically satisfy any of these separate approval gates.  Missing thresholds, unapproved schemas, incomplete datasets, undefined permissions or insufficient evidence must remain explicitly pending.  No missing decision may be interpreted as implicit approval.  7. FIRST-RELEASE ACCEPTANCE PRINCIPLE  The first release should demonstrate that SupportIQ can operate within its defined synthetic/local-only boundary, enforce established security and lifecycle restrictions, produce structured and traceable AI outputs, and expose measurable evaluation evidence.  It must not claim production readiness, contractual SLA compliance, unrestricted portability or live-integration safety without the corresponding independently verified evidence and approvals.  8. FINAL RATIONALE  The selected approach prioritizes controlled product demonstration, measurable quality, tenant isolation, data integrity, human decision authority and explicit governance.  Technical implementation and future portability must follow verified requirements and approved evidence rather than assumptions.  The unresolved items listed above remain formal decision and approval gates.  All previously established Q1-Q7 restrictions and Q8 decisions remain unchanged.  This response records clarification decisions only. It does not approve the PRD, authorize implementation, authorize test execution, grant runtime or connector permissions, authorize deployment or approve production release.

evaluation_metrics.exact_rendered_segment: Q8 — EVALUATION METRICS, DATASET AND BASELINE  1. EVALUATION OBJECTIVE  The first release must establish a measurable and reproducible quality-evaluation framework for SupportIQ using synthetic/local-only evaluation data.  The evaluation must measure model quality, classification quality, citation reliability, structured-output validity, security enforcement, lifecycle enforcement, and response latency.  Model quality must be measured independently from human acceptance or override rates.  No metric may be declared passed without an explicitly defined scoring method, eligible denominator, evaluation dataset, and recorded evidence.  2. GROUNDED ANSWER QUALITY  Grounded-answer evaluation must measure whether generated answers are supported by eligible and authorized knowledge sources.  Each evaluated response must be assessed for:  - Factual support from retrieved sources. - Relevance to the user question. - Absence of unsupported factual claims. - Consistency with the available source material. - Compliance with applicable tenant and lifecycle restrictions.  The expected answer and supporting evidence must be defined in the evaluation dataset.  A response containing unsupported material claims must not be classified as fully grounded.  The exact scoring rubric and minimum acceptance threshold require explicit approval before the release gate can pass.  3. CITATION CORRECTNESS  Citation evaluation must establish whether each citation:  - References an existing source. - Identifies the correct document and relevant passage. - Supports the associated factual claim. - Belongs to the authorized tenant. - References knowledge eligible for AI retrieval at the evaluation anchor. - Does not reference expired, rejected, superseded, overdue, or deletion-approved content.  Citation correctness must be evaluated independently from answer relevance.  Invalid, unsupported, inaccessible, or incorrectly attributed citations must be counted as failures.  Citation scoring must use an explicitly defined eligible citation population.  4. ABSTENTION AND CONFLICT HANDLING  The evaluation dataset must include:  - Questions with insufficient supporting knowledge. - Questions with conflicting authoritative sources. - Questions outside the available knowledge scope. - Questions involving unauthorized tenant content. - Questions involving expired, overdue, or otherwise ineligible knowledge.  The evaluation must measure whether the assistant correctly abstains, explains insufficient evidence, or requests human review where required.  A confident but unsupported answer must count as an evaluation failure.  The system must not resolve restricted knowledge conflicts merely by generating an answer.  Human-review and lifecycle restrictions remain mandatory.  5. CLASSIFICATION QUALITY  Category, Priority, and Queue suggestion quality must be evaluated independently.  Each field must have an explicitly labelled expected synthetic reference value.  Measure:  - Category suggestion accuracy. - Priority suggestion accuracy. - Queue suggestion accuracy. - Missing or unassessed suggestion rates. - Invalid or unsupported suggestion rates.  Only eligible records with a valid reference label may enter the applicable accuracy denominator.  Unassessed and ineligible records must be reported separately.  Model prediction accuracy must not be confused with human acceptance, rejection, or override rates defined in Q7.  6. STRUCTURED-OUTPUT VALIDITY  All required structured outputs must be evaluated against their approved schemas.  Evaluation must include:  - Valid JSON or required output format. - Required field presence. - Correct field types. - Allowed enumeration values. - Required-field validation. - Null and missing-value handling. - Rejection of malformed or unsupported values.  Schema-valid output and semantically correct output must be reported as separate quality dimensions.  The evaluation schema must be version-controlled.  Undefined schema fields and validation requirements remain gated until explicitly approved.  7. TENANT ISOLATION AND LIFECYCLE ENFORCEMENT  Tenant isolation must be evaluated through positive and negative authorization tests.  The evaluation must verify that:  - Authorized tenant users can access only permitted tenant resources. - Cross-tenant document and knowledge retrieval is denied. - Unauthorized citations cannot expose another tenant's information. - Platform Admin permissions do not grant tenant-content access. - Restricted lifecycle states are excluded from AI retrieval and citation. - Overdue, rejected, expired, superseded, and deletion-approved knowledge cannot become eligible through an unrelated operation.  These are mandatory security and lifecycle evaluation dimensions.  Any confirmed unauthorized cross-tenant access or prohibited lifecycle retrieval must be treated as a release-blocking failure.  Passing average model-quality metrics must never compensate for security or lifecycle failures.  8. RESPONSE LATENCY EVALUATION  The first release may measure descriptive response latency using synthetic evaluation scenarios.  Report: - Median response latency (P50). - 95th percentile response latency (P95). - Evaluation sample count. - Evaluation environment. - Model and configuration version. - Relevant test conditions.  Latency must be measured using explicitly recorded timestamps and a consistent measurement boundary.  These are descriptive measurements, not production performance guarantees or contractual SLAs.  Minimum latency targets and production performance commitments remain deferred.  9. SYNTHETIC EVALUATION DATASET  Create a version-controlled synthetic evaluation dataset.  The dataset must contain:  - Evaluation case identifier. - Synthetic tenant identifier. - Input question or classification scenario. - Expected answer or reference classification. - Expected supporting source references. - Expected abstention or human-review behaviour, where applicable. - Expected structured-output schema. - Applicable lifecycle and authorization conditions. - Evaluation category and difficulty. - Expected outcome and scoring rubric.  Include normal, edge, negative, insufficient-evidence, conflicting-source, and unauthorized-access scenarios.  Every expected reference label must have identifiable provenance and review status.  The dataset must not contain real customer information or production tenant content.  Use an explicit dataset version, such as SupportIQ-Eval-v1.0.  Evaluation dataset changes must be version-controlled so that results from different versions are not silently compared as equivalent.  10. BASELINE AND SCORING GOVERNANCE  The initial evaluation baseline must be established through actual execution against an approved, versioned synthetic evaluation dataset.  Record:  - Dataset version. - Model and model configuration version. - Application build version. - Evaluation date and environment. - Metric definitions and scoring rubric versions. - Eligible population and denominators. - Raw evaluation results. - Excluded and invalid cases. - Failure classifications. - Evaluation evidence.  Aggregate scores must not hide field-level, tenant-isolation, citation, or lifecycle failures.  A baseline must not be invented or declared passed before the evaluation has actually been executed and independently reviewed.  11. HUMAN ACCEPTANCE VERSUS MODEL QUALITY  Model quality metrics and human decision metrics must remain separate.  Model quality measures the correctness of AI-generated answers and suggestions against independently prepared synthetic reference labels.  Human acceptance, rejection, and override rates measure completed human review decisions as defined in Q7-C02.  High human acceptance must not automatically establish model correctness.  Similarly, a model evaluation score must not replace independent human approval requirements.  12. QUALITY THRESHOLDS AND RELEASE GATES  Metric definitions and evaluation methodology are established first.  Numeric quality thresholds, minimum sample sizes, confidence requirements, and final release acceptance criteria must not be invented or assumed.  These values require explicit approval based on evaluation evidence and the intended release risk.  Until approved thresholds and corresponding evidence exist, the applicable quality gate must remain NOT EVALUATED or NOT APPROVED.  Security, tenant-isolation, authorization, and lifecycle enforcement failures are release-blocking regardless of aggregate model-quality scores.  13. EXPLICITLY DEFERRED ITEMS  The following remain deferred until separately defined and approved:  - Numeric model-quality acceptance thresholds. - Minimum evaluation sample sizes. - Statistical confidence requirements. - Production performance targets. - Production SLA commitments. - Actual customer-data evaluation. - Advanced model benchmarking. - Continuous production monitoring and drift thresholds. - Automated quality-based model promotion. - Production rollout and release authorization.  14. FINAL DECISION  The first release will establish a measurable evaluation framework using version-controlled synthetic/local-only data.  Grounded answers, citation correctness, abstention, classification quality, structured-output validity, tenant isolation, lifecycle enforcement, and response latency will be evaluated independently.  The initial baseline must come from actual recorded evaluation results, not assumed values.  Numeric acceptance thresholds and final release criteria remain explicit approval gates until supported by evidence and approved.  No quality gate may be marked passed merely because its metric, dataset, or test plan has been defined.  All Q1-Q7 security, authorization, tenant-isolation, lifecycle, retention, analytics, and no-external-action restrictions remain unchanged.  These decisions clarify evaluation requirements only. They do not authorize tests, implementation, PRD approval, or product release.,

numeric_thresholds.exact_rendered_segment: Q8-C02 — NUMERIC ACCEPTANCE THRESHOLDS AND APPROVAL AUTHORITY  1. NUMERIC QUALITY THRESHOLDS  Do not invent or assume numeric acceptance thresholds for the first release.  The following metrics require explicitly approved numeric pass/fail criteria:  - Grounded answer accuracy. - Citation correctness. - Correct abstention and conflict handling. - Category suggestion accuracy. - Priority suggestion accuracy. - Queue suggestion accuracy. - Structured-output validity. - Response latency, including P50 and P95.  These thresholds must be proposed using actual evaluation evidence, dataset characteristics, business risk and the approved scoring methodology.  Until independently approved, these values remain PENDING and the corresponding quality release gates must remain NOT EVALUATED / NOT APPROVED.  2. CRITICAL SECURITY AND SAFETY THRESHOLDS  The following are mandatory zero-tolerance release conditions:  - Confirmed cross-tenant data leakage. - Unauthorized tenant-content access. - Unauthorized knowledge retrieval or citation. - Retrieval of deletion-approved or otherwise prohibited knowledge. - Bypass of tenant authorization or lifecycle restrictions. - Platform Admin access to tenant content. - Unauthorized approval, reinstatement or privilege escalation.  Any confirmed critical violation is a release-blocking failure, regardless of aggregate quality scores or other passing metrics.  A zero-tolerance policy means zero confirmed violations in the applicable evaluation. It does not imply that finite testing mathematically proves the absence of every possible vulnerability.  3. SAMPLE SIZE AND TEST COVERAGE  Minimum evaluation sample sizes, category-wise coverage, negative-test coverage, statistical confidence requirements and test repetition criteria remain PENDING.  These must be proposed based on:  - Evaluation dataset size and representativeness. - Metric-specific eligible populations. - Risk and severity of failure. - Coverage of normal, boundary and negative scenarios. - Tenant-isolation and lifecycle test coverage. - Reproducibility of evaluation results.  A release must not be considered passed merely because a small or incomplete sample produces favourable results.  4. LATENCY ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA  P50 and P95 latency must be measured and recorded using a consistent measurement boundary.  Numeric latency targets, concurrency assumptions, load profiles, hardware/runtime environment and performance acceptance criteria remain PENDING.  Descriptive latency measurements must not be represented as production SLA commitments.  5. PROPOSAL AND INDEPENDENT APPROVAL AUTHORITY  The proposed governance arrangement is:  - Product Owner / Quality Owner: Proposes metric definitions, numeric acceptance thresholds, dataset coverage and evaluation methodology. - Independent Release Approver: Reviews the supporting evidence and independently approves or rejects the proposed quality acceptance criteria. - Security Owner: Independently reviews and approves security-critical acceptance criteria, including tenant isolation, authorization and lifecycle enforcement. - Engineering Team: Provides implementation evidence, test results and technical recommendations but cannot independently approve its own release acceptance results.  The person proposing a threshold must not be its sole final approver.  The exact accountable individuals and formal role assignments must be recorded before the relevant approval gate is activated.  Administrative privileges alone must not confer Knowledge Reviewer authority or tenant-content access.  6. RELEASE BLOCKING BOUNDARY  Until numeric quality thresholds, minimum sample sizes, evaluation coverage and independent approval authority are explicitly documented and approved:  - The relevant quality acceptance gate remains PENDING. - No missing threshold may be treated as an implicit pass. - No aggregate score may override a critical security failure. - No quality result may be represented as independently approved without recorded approval evidence. - Production release authorization remains separate from metric definition and evaluation planning.  7. EXPLICITLY DEFERRED DECISIONS  The following remain unresolved and require separate approval:  - Exact numeric thresholds for each quality metric. - Minimum evaluation sample sizes. - Statistical confidence and coverage requirements. - P50/P95 latency targets and load conditions. - Named individuals assigned to approval roles. - Final release acceptance criteria.  RATIONALE:  The first release should establish evidence-based quality governance rather than arbitrary numerical targets.  Security and authorization violations require zero-tolerance treatment, while model-quality thresholds should be based on reproducible evaluation results and independently approved acceptance criteria.  This decision records the intended governance boundary only. It does not approve the PRD, authorize implementation, approve testing execution or authorize product release.  All previously established Q1-Q7 restrictions remain unchanged.,

evidence_ownership.exact_rendered_segment: Q8-C03 — EVALUATION EVIDENCE OWNER AND CONFIGURATION BINDING  1. EVIDENCE PREPARATION  The Engineering and QA teams are responsible for preparing evaluation evidence.  They must execute the approved evaluation suite against the explicitly identified application build, model configuration, synthetic dataset and policy versions.  Evidence must include:  - Test execution records. - Evaluation dataset and version. - Metric definitions and scoring methodology. - Expected and actual results. - Pass/fail outcomes. - Failed and excluded test cases with reasons. - Security and lifecycle test results. - Relevant logs and reproducible execution references.  The team preparing evidence must not independently approve its own release evidence.  2. INDEPENDENT VERIFICATION AND REVIEW  An independent QA / Quality Reviewer must verify:  - Correctness and completeness of the evaluation execution. - Dataset and expected-reference integrity. - Scoring methodology and denominator calculations. - Reproducibility of reported results. - Correct application and configuration versions. - Completeness of failed, excluded and unresolved test cases. - Security and lifecycle evaluation evidence.  The reviewer must be independent of the evidence preparation and must not approve their own work.  3. EVIDENCE ACCEPTANCE AND RELEASE AUTHORITY  An authorized Independent Release Approver is responsible for accepting or rejecting the final evaluation evidence.  The Security Owner must independently review security-critical evidence, including tenant isolation, authorization and lifecycle enforcement.  The final human release decision must consider:  - Approved acceptance thresholds. - Verified evaluation evidence. - Critical security and lifecycle results. - Open defects and unresolved exceptions. - Applicable approval and SDLC gates.  Evidence acceptance does not itself authorize production deployment or implementation.  The exact named individuals and formal role assignments must be established through the applicable governance approval process.  4. CONFIGURATION BINDING  Every evaluation execution must be bound to an immutable configuration manifest containing, where applicable:  APPLICATION: - Application version and build identifier. - Git commit ID and relevant release candidate. - Relevant dependency and configuration versions.  AI MODEL: - AI provider. - Model name and exact model version. - Model parameters and relevant inference configuration.  PROMPT: - System prompt version. - Prompt template and configuration version. - Relevant generation settings.  RETRIEVAL AND KNOWLEDGE: - Retrieval configuration and parameters. - Embedding model and version. - Vector index version. - Chunking and indexing configuration. - Synthetic knowledge dataset version and snapshot identifier.  BUSINESS AND SECURITY POLICIES: - Taxonomy and category mapping version. - Priority and routing rule versions. - Tenant authorization policy version. - Knowledge lifecycle policy version.  EVALUATION: - Evaluation dataset version. - Test suite version. - Metric definition and scoring rubric versions. - Execution timestamp and environment. - Raw results and final evaluation report.  Sensitive credentials, secrets and actual customer content must never be included in evaluation evidence.  5. CONFIGURATION CHANGE AND RE-EVALUATION RULES  A new evaluation is required whenever a change materially affects the validity of previous evidence.  Examples include:  - AI provider, model or model-version changes. - System prompt or generation configuration changes. - Embedding, retrieval, indexing or chunking changes. - Knowledge source or evaluation dataset changes. - Taxonomy, priority or routing rule changes. - Tenant authorization or lifecycle policy changes. - Application changes affecting retrieval, answer generation, classification, security or evaluation behaviour.  The required re-evaluation scope must be determined through documented impact analysis.  Security, authorization and lifecycle changes must trigger the applicable security and lifecycle regression tests.  A change that invalidates previous evidence must not inherit an earlier passing result without fresh verification.  Evidence remains traceable to its original configuration even after newer versions are introduced.  6. FAILURE AND EXCEPTION HANDLING  Failed evaluations must remain recorded and must not be silently removed, overwritten or reported as passing.  Every failure must include:  - Test case identifier. - Affected metric or control. - Expected result. - Actual result. - Failure severity. - Relevant configuration. - Investigation status. - Corrective action and verification evidence.  Any exception requires documented justification, explicit scope and approval by the authorized human authority.  Critical security, tenant-isolation, authorization and prohibited-lifecycle failures cannot be waived through aggregate quality scores or informal exceptions.  Unresolved critical failures must block the applicable release gate.  7. EVIDENCE RETENTION AND TRACEABILITY  Evaluation evidence must be version-controlled and traceable to the exact configuration that produced it.  Evidence records must preserve their original execution context and approval history.  Evidence retention duration and detailed archival or purge implementation remain subject to the applicable retention policy and approval requirements.  No evidence may be modified retrospectively to conceal a failure or change an earlier approval decision.  8. SEPARATION OF SDLC GATES  The following activities remain separate:  - Evaluation planning. - Evaluation execution. - Independent evidence verification. - Acceptance of evaluation evidence. - Requirement approval. - Implementation authorization. - Production release authorization.  Completing one stage does not automatically approve or authorize the next stage.  No clarification or evidence acceptance in this question grants permission to begin implementation, modify the PRD, deploy software or initiate another SDLC process.  9. EXPLICITLY DEFERRED ITEMS  The following remain pending:  - Named individuals assigned to each governance role. - Final approval delegation and escalation arrangements. - Exact evidence retention duration. - Detailed configuration manifest schema. - Automated configuration-drift detection. - Automated re-evaluation and evidence invalidation workflows. - Formal release approval workflow and tooling.  RATIONALE:  The first release must provide reproducible, independently verifiable evaluation evidence.  Binding every result to its exact software, AI, prompt, retrieval, dataset and policy configuration prevents outdated test results from being incorrectly reused after material changes.  Independent verification and human release authority preserve separation of duties and SDLC governance.  All previously established Q1-Q7 restrictions and Q8 acceptance-threshold requirements remain unchanged.  These decisions clarify governance and evidence requirements only. They do not approve the PRD, authorize implementation, authorize test execution or approve production release.,

citations.exact_rendered_segment: Q8-C04 — CITATION IDENTITY, DISPLAY AND SAFE FALLBACK  1. STABLE CITATION IDENTITY  Every citation must reference a stable, tenant-scoped source identity.  The minimum identity must include:  - Tenant identifier. - Document identifier. - Exact document version identifier. - Source location identifier, where available. - Relevant page, section or chunk reference, where available.  A citation must resolve to the exact source version used during answer generation.  A document identifier alone is not sufficient to establish that the cited content supports an answer.  A citation must remain distinguishable from references to other versions of the same logical document.  2. HUMAN-READABLE CITATION DISPLAY  Where available and authorized, the user-facing citation should display:  - Document title. - Document version. - Relevant page number. - Section name. - Relevant source excerpt or supporting passage. - Accessible source reference.  Display metadata must be derived from the actual indexed document and its recorded metadata.  The system must never invent document titles, version numbers, page numbers, section names or source references.  3. MISSING OR INCOMPLETE METADATA  If a document title is unavailable, use a safe document reference only if that reference is authorized for display.  If a page number, section name or other location metadata is unavailable, explicitly indicate that the information is unavailable.  Do not substitute guessed page numbers, inferred section names or fabricated metadata.  If the source cannot be identified reliably, do not present the citation as verified.  4. SOURCE ACCESSIBILITY AND SAFE FALLBACK  Before displaying a citation or providing an accessible source link, verify that:  - The source belongs to the requesting tenant. - The requesting user is authorized to access it. - The exact cited version remains eligible for AI retrieval and citation. - The cited source location is valid. - The supporting evidence is available and actually supports the associated claim.  If the original source is unavailable, inaccessible, or cannot be verified, the assistant must not manufacture a replacement reference.  Where citation evidence is insufficient, the assistant must qualify the answer, abstain from unsupported claims or request human review as appropriate.  Human authorization to inspect a document is separate from AI retrieval and citation eligibility.  5. CITATION AND SOURCE-VERSION RESTRICTIONS  The assistant must never cite:  - Expired documents. - Rejected documents. - Superseded versions. - Overdue knowledge pending re-review. - Deletion-approved content. - Unauthorized tenant content. - Sources that fail applicable lifecycle or authorization checks.  A valid-looking document reference does not prove that its contents support the generated answer.  An older version must not be cited merely because it remains stored.  Existing Q1-Q5 lifecycle, approval, retention and deletion restrictions remain mandatory.  6. CITATION VALIDATION  Citation evaluation must independently verify:  - Correct tenant identity. - Correct document identity. - Correct document version. - Correct source location. - Actual support for the associated factual claim. - Current retrieval eligibility. - User authorization. - Source accessibility.  A citation that points to the correct document but an irrelevant or unsupported passage must be treated as incorrect.  Citation identity validity and citation evidence correctness must remain separate evaluation dimensions.  7. AUDITABILITY AND TRACEABILITY  Each generated citation must be traceable to its original retrieval context and exact document version.  Where applicable, retain:  - Citation identifier. - Tenant and document identifiers. - Document version. - Source location and chunk identifier. - Retrieval execution reference. - Citation validation outcome. - Applicable policy version.  Audit records must not expose confidential source content or unauthorized tenant metadata.  8. EXPLICITLY DEFERRED ITEMS  The following implementation details remain subject to further design and approval:  - Final citation display format. - Exact metadata schema. - Citation-link expiration and access-refresh behaviour. - Source excerpt display limits. - Behaviour when the original document is archived or physically unavailable. - Detailed citation audit retention implementation. - User-interface treatment of unavailable citations.  These details must not be filled with assumed defaults.  RATIONALE:  The first release must provide trustworthy, traceable and tenant-safe citations.  The system must prioritize source accuracy and authorization over displaying a citation for every generated answer.  A missing citation must never be replaced by fabricated metadata or an unauthorized alternative source.  All previously established Q1-Q7 restrictions and Q8 evaluation governance requirements remain unchanged.  This clarification does not approve the PRD, authorize implementation, testing execution or production release.,

structured_outputs.exact_rendered_segment: Q8-C05 — REQUIRED STRUCTURED RESPONSE CONTRACTS  1. FIRST-RELEASE RESPONSE TYPES  The first release must define versioned structured response contracts for the following response types:  A. ANSWER / ABSTENTION - Generated answer. - Supporting evidence references. - Citation references. - Evidence sufficiency status. - Uncertainty indicators. - Abstention reason, where applicable. - Human-review requirement.  B. SUMMARY - Summary text. - Source document and version references. - Supporting evidence references. - Missing or unavailable information indicators. - Uncertainty or qualification markers.  C. CATEGORY SUGGESTION - Suggested category identifier and value. - Explanation. - Supporting evidence. - Confidence or uncertainty indicator. - Human-review status.  D. PRIORITY SUGGESTION - Suggested priority value. - Explanation and supporting evidence. - Confidence or uncertainty indicator. - Human-review status.  E. QUEUE SUGGESTION - Suggested synthetic/local queue identifier. - Explanation and supporting evidence. - Uncertainty indicator. - Human-review status.  F. ESCALATION RECOMMENDATION - Whether human escalation is recommended. - Reason and supporting evidence. - Suggested escalation category, where defined. - Uncertainty and review requirements.  Escalation recommendations must never automatically modify tickets, queues, assignments or external systems.  2. COMMON REQUIRED RESPONSE FIELDS  Where applicable, every structured response must include:  - ResponseId. - ResponseType. - SchemaVersion. - ResponseStatus. - SuggestedValue. - Explanation. - EvidenceReferences. - CitationReferences. - ConfidenceIndicator, where supported. - UncertaintyMarkers. - HumanReviewRequired. - GeneratedTimestamp. - Applicable tenant and authorization context.  Fields must be appropriate to the response type.  Unavailable values must be represented explicitly according to the approved schema rather than fabricated or silently substituted.  3. STATUS VALUES AND SEMANTICS  The following status values are proposed:  - SUGGESTED: AI-generated recommendation. - NEEDS_REVIEW: Human review is required. - ACCEPTED: Explicitly accepted by an authorized human reviewer. - REJECTED: Explicitly rejected by an authorized human reviewer. - OVERRIDDEN: An authorized human has replaced the suggested value. - UNASSESSED: Insufficient information to make an assessment. - ABSTAINED: The assistant deliberately abstained from providing an unsupported answer.  AI-generated responses may create SUGGESTED, NEEDS_REVIEW, UNASSESSED or ABSTAINED outcomes as applicable.  ACCEPTED, REJECTED and OVERRIDDEN must originate only from authorized human decisions.  An AI suggestion must never be represented as an authoritative human decision.  4. EVIDENCE, UNCERTAINTY AND REVIEW MARKERS  Every response must distinguish:  - Supported claims. - Unsupported or insufficiently supported claims. - Missing source information. - Conflicting evidence. - Unavailable citations. - Restricted or ineligible knowledge. - Human-review requirements.  Confidence indicators must not be interpreted as proof of factual correctness.  Where evidence is insufficient or conflicting, the assistant must qualify its response, abstain or request human review as appropriate.  Restricted tenant content and lifecycle-ineligible knowledge must never be used to populate response evidence.  5. STRICT SCHEMA VALIDATION  All structured responses must be validated against their exact approved, versioned schemas.  Validation must cover:  - Required fields. - Field data types. - Allowed enumerations. - Null and missing-value behaviour. - Response-type-specific requirements. - Evidence and citation references. - Status transition restrictions. - Tenant and authorization context. - Schema version compatibility.  Malformed, incomplete or unsupported outputs must not be silently accepted.  A schema-valid response must not automatically be considered factually correct.  Schema validation and semantic evaluation must remain separate quality dimensions.  6. SCHEMA VERSIONING AND APPROVAL  Each response contract must have an explicit version identifier.  Schema definitions, allowed enums, required fields and validation rules must be version-controlled.  The exact response schemas and their approval status must be established before affected implementation and formal evaluation proceed.  Changes to an approved schema must be versioned and assessed for backward compatibility.  A material schema change must trigger the applicable regression and evaluation activities.  No implementation or evaluation gate may assume an unapproved schema.  7. HUMAN DECISION AND AUTOMATION BOUNDARIES  AI-generated structured responses are recommendations only.
