The assistant must not automatically:  - Accept or reject knowledge. - Approve document versions. - Change authoritative classifications. - Update ticket fields. - Change ticket ownership or assignments. - Modify external queues. - Trigger escalation workflows. - Send outgoing messages. - Perform external write operations.  All authoritative decisions must remain with the appropriately authorized human roles established in Q2, Q3, Q4 and Q6.  Human decisions must be independently auditable and distinguishable from original AI suggestions.  8. FIRST-RELEASE TAXONOMY AND ENUM DEPENDENCIES  Category, Priority and Queue enumerations must reference the approved Q6 taxonomy and mapping definitions.  Do not invent or hardcode unapproved category, priority or queue values.  Unsupported, ambiguous or unavailable values must be represented through explicitly approved fallback or UNASSESSED behaviour.  The response schema must not independently create new business categories or bypass Q6 approval requirements.  9. EXPLICITLY DEFERRED ITEMS  The following require separate design and approval:  - Exact JSON Schema definitions. - Final schema versions. - Complete response-type-specific field definitions. - Final enum values and fallback mappings. - Confidence-score representation and calibration. - Detailed error-response contracts. - Backward-compatibility and migration rules. - Exact schema approval roles. - Automated schema compatibility testing.  Until approved, affected implementation and evaluation must remain gated.  RATIONALE:  Structured response contracts provide predictable, machine-validatable AI outputs while preserving the distinction between AI recommendations and authoritative human decisions.  Strict schema validation improves integration reliability, auditability and future extensibility.  Separating output structure from decision authority prevents AI-generated suggestions from silently becoming operational actions.  All Q1-Q7 restrictions and Q8 evaluation governance requirements remain unchanged.  These decisions clarify requirements only. They do not approve the PRD, authorize implementation, testing execution or production release.,

retry_rejection.exact_rendered_segment: Q8-C06 — SAFE RETRY, REJECTION AND FAILURE VISIBILITY  1. GENERAL FAILURE-HANDLING PRINCIPLE  The first release must follow a fail-safe approach.  When an operation cannot be completed reliably, the system must explicitly report failure, abstain or request human review rather than fabricate success or return unsupported results.  Retry must be bounded and permitted only for explicitly classified transient failures.  Security, authorization, tenant-isolation and lifecycle restrictions must never be bypassed during retry or recovery.  2. FAILURES PERMITTING BOUNDED RETRY  The following transient failures may permit a bounded retry:  - Temporary network interruptions. - AI provider transient service errors. - Temporary provider rate limiting. - Transient dependency unavailability. - Recoverable infrastructure timeouts.  Retries must use an explicitly approved retry policy with configurable limits, appropriate backoff and timeout handling.  Idempotency and duplicate-request protection must be maintained wherever applicable.  Exact retry counts, backoff intervals, timeout values and circuit-breaker thresholds remain pending technical design and approval.  3. INVALID SCHEMA AND MALFORMED OUTPUT  If an AI response fails structured schema validation:  - Reject the invalid output. - A bounded corrective retry may be considered where safe and supported. - Revalidate the complete response against the exact approved schema. - Do not expose malformed output as a successful response. - Do not silently discard missing required fields or invent replacement values.  If validation continues to fail, mark the operation as FAILED and expose an appropriate error or human-review requirement.  Schema-valid output must still undergo applicable semantic and evidence validation.  4. MISSING CITATIONS AND INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE  Missing, invalid or unsupported citations must not be treated as successful grounded answers.  If citation evidence is unavailable:  - Abstain from unsupported factual claims. - Return an appropriately qualified response where partial support exists. - Identify missing evidence where possible. - Request human review when required.  Insufficient or conflicting evidence must not trigger unlimited retries or automatic selection of an unsupported source.  5. SECURITY, AUTHORIZATION AND LIFECYCLE FAILURES  The following conditions require immediate rejection or blocking without retry:  - Unauthorized access. - Cross-tenant access attempts. - Tenant authorization failures. - Prohibited lifecycle-state retrieval. - Expired, rejected or superseded knowledge. - Overdue knowledge excluded from AI retrieval. - Deletion-approved content. - Unauthorized approval or reinstatement attempts.  These conditions must not be converted into transient errors.  No retry, fallback, alternate provider or reprocessing mechanism may bypass authorization, tenant isolation, deletion or lifecycle controls.  Confirmed security violations must be recorded for appropriate security investigation and escalation.  6. UNAVAILABLE DEPENDENCIES  If the AI provider, retrieval service, vector index, database or another required dependency becomes unavailable:  - Do not report successful processing without verified completion. - Permit bounded retries only for classified transient failures. - Return a clear service-unavailable or processing-failed outcome. - Preserve the request correlation identifier. - Avoid duplicate processing or inconsistent partial results. - Expose the failure to authorized operational personnel.  If a required dependency remains unavailable, the affected operation must remain FAILED or otherwise explicitly unresolved.  7. DELETION AND PURGE SAFEGUARDS  Deletion-approved content must never be reprocessed or restored through retry, recovery, indexing or alternate processing paths.  A failed purge must remain visibly incomplete.  Retry ownership, escalation and deletion verification must follow the approved Q5 deletion and retention requirements.  The system must never report successful deletion before the applicable deletion operation has been verified.  8. FAILURE STATUS AND VISIBILITY  The system must distinguish at least the following operational outcomes:  - SUCCESS: Operation completed and validated. - RETRYING: A permitted transient retry is in progress. - FAILED: Operation could not be completed. - REJECTED: Input or operation was rejected by validation or policy. - ABSTAINED: Assistant deliberately declined to provide an unsupported answer. - NEEDS_REVIEW: Human intervention is required. - BLOCKED: Operation was prevented by authorization, security or lifecycle restrictions.  These operational statuses must remain separate from authoritative knowledge lifecycle and human approval statuses.  A technical retry must not automatically change an approval or lifecycle decision.  9. FAILURE VISIBILITY AND AUDITABILITY  For end users, provide a clear and safe explanation of the failure, including whether retry or human review is appropriate.  For authorized administrators and support personnel, record:  - Correlation ID and request identifier. - Failure category and error code. - Relevant operation and dependency. - Timestamp. - Retry attempt information. - Final processing status. - Applicable configuration version. - Resolution or escalation status.  Do not expose credentials, API keys, confidential source content, internal secrets or unauthorized tenant information in error messages or logs.  Failure logs must be tenant-safe and accessible only to appropriately authorized roles.  10. EXPLICITLY DEFERRED ITEMS  The following require separate technical definition and approval:  - Exact retry counts. - Backoff intervals. - Provider-specific timeout values. - Circuit-breaker configuration. - Retry ownership and operational escalation. - Dead-letter and failed-request handling. - Detailed error-code catalogue. - Automated recovery workflows. - Failure-log retention and monitoring thresholds.  Until approved, these values must not be silently assumed or treated as implemented guarantees.  RATIONALE:  The first release must prioritize correctness, security and transparent failure handling over uninterrupted processing.  Transient technical failures may receive bounded retries, while authorization, tenant-isolation, lifecycle and deletion violations require immediate blocking.  An explicit failure or abstention is preferable to an apparently successful but unsupported answer.  All previously established Q1-Q7 restrictions and Q8 evaluation requirements remain unchanged.  These decisions clarify requirements only. They do not approve the PRD, authorize implementation, testing execution or production release.,

rationale_deferrals.exact_rendered_segment: Q8-C07 — RATIONALE AND EXPLICIT UNRESOLVED RELEASE GATES  1. FIRST-RELEASE POLICY AND RATIONALE  The first demonstrable release of SupportIQ must remain within the previously established synthetic/local-only, read-only and restricted integration boundary.  The purpose of this release is to demonstrate the core product capabilities while establishing measurable quality, security, governance and operational evidence.  The first release may demonstrate:  - AI-generated answers and summaries using eligible synthetic knowledge. - Tenant-scoped knowledge retrieval and citation. - Category, Priority and Queue suggestions. - Human-review and approval workflows. - Structured response validation. - Synthetic analytics and evaluation reporting. - Safe failure, abstention and bounded retry behaviour.  The system must not introduce real customer data, unrestricted production integrations, automatic ticket changes, outgoing messages or unauthorized external actions.  These restrictions provide a controlled environment in which the product can be evaluated without assuming that synthetic demonstrations prove production readiness.  2. QUALITY AND EVALUATION POLICY  Evaluation must be based on version-controlled synthetic datasets and explicitly defined scoring methodology.  Actual evaluation results must be recorded and independently reviewed.  No numeric quality threshold, performance target, statistical confidence level or minimum sample size may be invented or assumed.  Security, tenant isolation, authorization and lifecycle violations remain mandatory release-blocking conditions.  A favourable aggregate model-quality score cannot compensate for a critical security or authorization failure.  3. EVIDENCE AND CONFIGURATION GOVERNANCE  Evaluation evidence must be bound to the exact application build, Git commit, AI provider/model version, prompt configuration, retrieval settings, dataset version, taxonomy and applicable policy versions.  Evidence must be independently verified and accepted by authorized human roles.  Material configuration changes must trigger impact assessment and the applicable re-evaluation.  Acceptance of evaluation evidence remains separate from Requirement approval, implementation authorization and production release approval.  4. EXPLICITLY UNRESOLVED DECISIONS  The following decisions remain pending and must not be silently assumed:  A. QUALITY AND EVALUATION - Numeric pass/fail thresholds for each applicable quality metric. - Minimum evaluation sample sizes and coverage. - Statistical confidence and acceptance requirements. - P50/P95 latency targets and load conditions. - Final quality acceptance criteria.  B. RESPONSE CONTRACTS AND DATASETS - Exact approved structured-response schemas and versions. - Final taxonomy and enum definitions where not already approved. - Complete synthetic evaluation dataset and reference-label approval. - Final citation metadata and display contracts. - Detailed error and failure-response contracts.  C. GOVERNANCE AND PERMISSIONS - Named individuals assigned to evidence preparation, independent verification, security review and release approval. - Final approval delegation and escalation arrangements. - Exact permissions for any future runtime or live integration. - Formal evidence acceptance and release authorization records.  D. TECHNICAL AND OPERATIONAL POLICY - Retry counts, backoff and timeout settings. - Final latency and performance acceptance conditions. - Detailed monitoring and recovery arrangements. - Evidence retention and archival implementation. - Automated configuration-drift and re-evaluation mechanisms.  E. RETENTION AND LIFECYCLE - Previously deferred Q5 retention schedules and affected capability approval gates remain unresolved. - No retention deferral implies permission to retain, retrieve or reprocess prohibited content.  5. PB-02 PORTABILITY CONDITION  PB-02 remains an explicit unresolved approval gate.  The synthetic/local-only boundary does not automatically establish that the system is safe or authorized for runtime, production, external-provider or live-integration operation.  Before any affected runtime, live integration or release boundary proceeds, the following must be explicitly defined and approved:  - Exact connector/provider permissions. - Exact permitted data reads and operations. - Tenant and user authorization boundaries. - Applicable approved quality thresholds. - Required security and evaluation evidence. - Independent verification and approval records. - Applicable failure, retry and lifecycle safeguards.  No write, message-sending or external-action permission may be inferred from a read-only or synthetic demonstration.  If these conditions are not satisfied, the affected capability must remain blocked or deferred.  6. RELEASE GATE ENFORCEMENT  The following boundaries must remain separate:  - Requirement clarification. - Requirement approval. - Technical design approval. - Implementation authorization. - Test execution authorization. - Evaluation evidence acceptance. - Runtime and live-integration authorization. - Production deployment and release approval.  Completion of Q8 does not automatically satisfy any of these separate approval gates.  Missing thresholds, unapproved schemas, incomplete datasets, undefined permissions or insufficient evidence must remain explicitly pending.  No missing decision may be interpreted as implicit approval.  7. FIRST-RELEASE ACCEPTANCE PRINCIPLE  The first release should demonstrate that SupportIQ can operate within its defined synthetic/local-only boundary, enforce established security and lifecycle restrictions, produce structured and traceable AI outputs, and expose measurable evaluation evidence.  It must not claim production readiness, contractual SLA compliance, unrestricted portability or live-integration safety without the corresponding independently verified evidence and approvals.  8. FINAL RATIONALE  The selected approach prioritizes controlled product demonstration, measurable quality, tenant isolation, data integrity, human decision authority and explicit governance.  Technical implementation and future portability must follow verified requirements and approved evidence rather than assumptions.  The unresolved items listed above remain formal decision and approval gates.  All previously established Q1-Q7 restrictions and Q8 decisions remain unchanged.  This response records clarification decisions only. It does not approve the PRD, authorize implementation, authorize test execution, grant runtime or connector permissions, authorize deployment or approve production release.
